Supervision as Experience

Benjamin Wolstein Ph.D.

Benjamin Wolstein

Benjamin Wolstein, Ph.D.
2 West 67 Street
New York, N.Y. 10023

Benjamin Wolstein  

MOST DIFFICULTIES in supervision, it is widely agreed, arise from difficulties in the therapy being studied. They arise, however, from two distinct sources that are often confused—psychological and metapsychological. That is, from the personalities of a particular supervisor and therapist studying the treatment of a particular patient; and from the demarcated boundaries of the field of supervision.

I deal mainly here with the difficulties from the second source and refer to the first only as illustration. For it is also becoming increasingly clear that the second are harder to penetrate in supervision because they reflect the very same difficulties in established models of psychoanalysis.

I will not discuss how best to train students in general, or how best to perceive the therapist's distortions converging with his patient's. I limit my comments to critical aspects of the field of supervision itself that make such perceptions possible.

Take as our point of reference that the patient needs direct inquiry and experience rather than interpretation of his values and behavior for a genuinely psychological therapy. And consider the following question: does his therapist also need direct inquiry and experience rather than evaluation of his treatment plan and procedure for a genuinely psychological supervision of that therapy?

Recently, two very different students raised this issue in an interesting way.

Minor changes have been made in this paper since it was presented at the weekly staff meeting of the Clinical Services, W. A. White Institute of Psychiatry, Psychoanalysis and Psychology, on May 18, 1971.

John Schimel  

HARRY STACK SULLIVAN (1940) has stressed the point that the feeling of Power, in the sense of having influence in interpersonal situations with significant others, is crucial for the maintenance of a sense of self-esteem in the individual and, subsequently, for the development of emotional (interpersonal) maturity. This proposition proves to be essentially reciprocating in that it posits influence in interpersonal affairs as an ingredient for growth as well as, derivatively, the ability to accept the needs and wishes, i.e., the influence of others, as hygienic factors in interpersonal situations. In these terms, the definition of maturity as the opportunity to exercise influence and the ability, in turn, to be influenced by the legitimate wishes and needs, not to mention apprehensions and fears, of others can be seen as an expression of an essentially humanistic and democratic stance. In a parallel manner, Erich Fromm's description of the authoritarian character as pathological and deviant is also an expression of a basically humanistic stance. The development of this theme in Escape from Freedom(Fromm, 1941) leaves little doubt that maturity from this point of view is neither widespread nor easily maintained.

Marianne Eckardt  

Bernard Landis and Edward S. Tauber, Eds.: In the Name of Life: Essays in Honor of Erich Fromm

New York: Holt, Rhinehart and Winston, 1972.

THERE COME MOMENTS in our lives when a clear event makes us aware of our acquiescence to mediocrity. Such event may be the suprise of the fresh smell of the country when we leave the stale, polluted atmosphere of the city. The event may be a well-tended front patch garden amid the weedy neglect that has crept into city streets, expressing contempt for the passersby. The event may be the taste of a good bread that reaffirms how delicious this daily staple can be, or a movie that electrifies us with its opening flash, as we know instantaneously that here is quality. So it is with a book that hits the mark of what it undertakes and fills us with joy and gratitude for just that quality of performance.

Thus the book In the Name of Life: Essays in Honor of Fromm, edited by Landis and Tauber. I am not referring to the quality of the collected essays, though many of them are outstanding, but to the inspiration of having found a concept of honoring Fromm, which so well reflects the essential core of Fromm's message. Already the title of the book, "In the Name of Life, " gives the reader the frame of reference which gives meaning to everything else. Fromm knows we are, as human beings, caught in the balance between destructive bondage and creative freedom. He believes in the vision of our potential for a creative, productive, and loving existence. But he also knows that we can meander down the wrong road.

Ari Kiev. Transcultural Psychiatry.

New York: The Free Press. 1972. 223 pages.

MODERN TECHNOLOGY—the ease of travel and mass media—has brought psychiatrists in technologically advanced countries face to face with mental disorders in developing countries. Differences noted, perhaps in frequency and certainly in symptomatology aroused their interest and resulted in the development of a new subfield of psychiatry labelled transcultural psychiatry. This subfield concerns itself with the relevance of cultural factors to differences in the frequency and nature of mental disorders and to their treatment on comparison of at least two cultures. Psychiatrists, cultural anthropologists and epidemiologists have played an active part in the development of this field.

Concurrently as cultural anthropology emerged from its initial descriptive phase and the number of remote, isolated, primitive cultures dwindled, a rapprochement between cultural anthropologists and psychoanalysts took place, attempts were made to bridge cultural anthropological and psychoanalytical concepts and psychoanalytic theory was increasingly employed to understand and to interpret sociocultural processes. As I have stated somewhere else: None of the disciplines involved in transcultural psychiatry—cultural anthropology, descriptive psychiatry and epidemiology—can adequately explain the phenomena observed in terms of their own discipline alone but a combined approach based on social science theory and psychoanalytic theory is required.

Ralph Crowley

Ralph Crowley  

Edith Weigert, M.D.: The Courage to Love: Selected Papers of … New Haven and London: Yale University Press, 1970. 421 pages, $15.

AS LONG AS there are Edith Weigerts living, teaching, and writing, psychoanalysis cannot die. Throughout these twenty-three selected papers, the same way she gives the human condition priority over psychopathology, she commits herself to being a human being before being a psychoanalyst.

It is therefore no accident that the first group of papers in this welcomed volume is subtitled, "Facing the Human Condition." Many of her other papers also could be included under this heading. Since the human condition involves life, love, death, human vulnerability, powerlessness, loneliness, and creativity, her trenchant discussions of psychoanalytic dynamics include copious references to those aspects of human existence. People, including analysts, are never static; they oscillate dynamically between polarities, such as the transferential and non-transferential aspects of a relationship.

What keeps Weigert's discussions of psychoanalysis full of vitality is her frank love affair with philosophy, unlike Freud's attitude toward it. "Psychoanalysts look at individual trees, philosophers at the whole woods, " she writes (p. xix). Thus she values philosophy's contribution in these words: "Scientific specialties which lose their philosophic moorings are likely to become scientific techniques" (p. 358).

Leon Salzman M.D.

Leon Salzman

Leon Salzman, M.D.
110 Riverside Drive
New York, New York 10024

Leon Salzman  

DR. SCHIMEL'S VIEW of the obsessional process illuminates aspects of its role in human behavior in a manner that is refreshing and enlightening. This phenomenon in man is so fascinating, confusing, infuriating and instructive that there are endless ways of observing, interpreting and hypothesizing about it that are valid and informative. Some theorists and observers focus or emphasize those features that their own preconceptions and predilections direct them towards. Others are more impressed with attacking the old and formulating new explanatory conceptions. Still others merely amass more data to confirm existing theory and to underwrite their own flagging convictions. Consequently, some add to a fresh view while others merely obsess and clutter up old ideas with more explanations. We all like to think that we fit in the more enlightened and progressive categories of observers while too often we fit in the mold of the exegete. I believe that Dr. Schimel fits the former category since he occasionally agrees with me and his views are provocative and stimulating.

Dr. Schimel insists that the tendency to label personality configurations in terms like obsessional or hysterical often defeats the main purpose of understanding the underlying dynamics. I agree with him most heartily as do many behavioral theorists who are trying to get away from the historically restricting medical model of syndromes, diseases, monocausal etiologies and the like. We now are inclined to think in terms of reaction types, or adaptive techniqus in which the whole gamut of personality devices, techniques and defenses are employed in the individual's effort to achieve and sustain some viable interaction and self-sustaining mode of living. However, when certain defenses form the core of the individual's functioning or become the major techniques in his integrative activities, then we can acknowledge this fact without implying or conveying a specific disease process. Thus we do acknowledge neurotic developments and can identify major modes of defense that allow us to call one an obsessional neurosis and another an hysterical neurosis.

I have also found that the dream of the obsessional may present a "sudden, unexpected and uncluttered discovery of how each of us is seen and experienced, " one in which there may be a "free breakthrough of feelings attitudes, and anticipations." THE TERM compulsion neurosis has often been used without sufficient care and discrimination. Kraepelin classified compulsive neuroses with the manic-depressions. Bleuler ascribed them to the schizophrenias. In psychoanalytic literature, however, we find the concept of the compulsive neurosis described as a genuine neurosis. To the Editors:

I would like to express some of my ambivalent feelings toward Jacque Lacan's theories. I have recently attempted to incorporate some of Lacan's concepts into my work on verbal and non-verbal resistance, and some elements have been quite useful.

I have, however, noticed that Dr. Mannoni (This Journal, volume 8, No. 1) and other disciples of Lacan seem to be overly defensive in their presentation of the material. Translations are typically prefaced with, "The material suffers in translation, " or " Ecrits is not easy to read." It would seem to me that if Lacan understands language's relationship to the imaginary, symbolic, and real, then he should be able to analyze his own material and discover why it is so difficult to link his concepts with language.

IN THIS PAPER Henry Ezriel makes use of material previously published (1950, 1951, 1952) and re-presented and published again after 1956, when this one in slightly longer form appeared. In some of these he refers to his work as analytic group treatment, in others as scientific testing of psychoanalytic theory and practice.

Ezriel is part of the British school of group therapists who, in doing analytic work in the group setting, tend to treat the group as if it were one patient, and to seek unifying themes, assumptions, and trends in the interaction of the members. He is paleo-Freudian in that he restricts his, the therapist's activity to two basic tenets. First, everything the patients say or do is related to the therapist. Second, the only intervention of the leader is to interpret, and with each interpretation to focus on and reinforce the view that all intrapsychic and interpersonal behavior of all the patients is always therapist-oriented, always transferential.

From the point of view of analytic group therapy, Ezriel is out of touch with the American tradition that tends to deemphasize the significance of the leader by stressing the importance of peer relations and real and projected peer interactions, and ego functions (Platt, 1970) ; (Schwartz and Wolf, 1969). This trend is most clearly to be seen in the alternate session, the regular meeting of the members of a treatment group without the physical presence of the therapist. Here the hierarchical vector is attenuated in reality. Moreover, transference, which even for Ezriel is ubiquitous, must be present also in peer interaction. Therefore, American analytic group therapists give due consideration to multiple and peripheral transference phenomena which occur among the members of the group (Wolf and Schwartz, 1962).

Unlike the British, American analytic group therapists tend to place less emphasis on group dynamics and more on individual uniqueness, individual differences, by seeking psychodynamic, latent motivation in bipersonal, tripersonal and multipersonal behavior. In looking at such behavior American group therapists tend to seek to understand the real and projected (symbolic) provocations for the real and projected (symbolic) responses among the members.

HISTORY has been called that study which tries to make sense of the past because the past did not make sense while it was happening. Predicting the future is much the same undertaking about the present; foretelling is an effort to make sense of the senselessness of the present, to make uncertainty certainty, to make complexity simple, and to motivate either through fear or hope those who would be apathetic. All this is done with the consciousness that we never know where we are until we have passed through that point. The proverb is "Truth is the Daughter of Time."

With all this limitation, there always has been an interest in the future. At times it has been taken for granted. At the present moment, dismay and concern about the future are growing. The fruits of technology and materialism—and yes, reason—are spoiling before our very eyes. Everything is speeded up beyond our ken. Everything is in flux. We have done things, accomplished much, accumulated much information and knowledge without knowing quite how or for what reason we have been of the Age of Reason; to what avail! Historically we are in the position of the late Renaissance men who did without knowing precisely why. It was only the post-Renaissance scholars, poets, and dramatists who attributed to the Renaissance doers a level of consciousness they did not have while they were doing.

6 Claremont Rd.

David Schecter  

ONE OF THE most striking psychological portrayals in the film "Devi" is nothing less than that of the whole life cycle. Besides laying out before us, in exquisite aesthetic taste, various characters representing different stages of the life cycle, the artistic presentation induces within us an experience of the major issues of development—birth, sickness, death, marriage, fertility, attachment, rebellion, individuation and detachment—to name a few.

185

One of the functions of great art, as of psychoanalysis, is to bring one step closer to psychic integration those elements of experience that have been dissociated from one another. During and after seeing this movie, one can feel one's own childlike playfulness and terror in the nephew Khoki, adolescent loneliness and choice of destinies in Doya, the sensuality and separateness of the young couple, the frustration and alienation of mother from her child, the unresolved dependency on father of the older son, the struggle for emancipation from father's authority and power by the younger son, and, most poignantly, the failure of the old man to achieve the culturally prescribed mastery of old age—namely, detachment from family through spiritual reunion with the gods. As the canvas is painted leisurely by the camera, one can feel consciously what is unconsciously probably a universal phenomenon—that is, the condensation of past experience, futuristic expectation, and hope as caught in the time slice of the present.

I would postulate that by age five to six most children begin to have a sense of what is deeply expected of them, not only in terms of good and bad behavior, but in the images and ideals of who they are to become. Ruth Moulton spells out the conflict-ridden destinies that befall the heroine, leading to her psychotic break. I have in mind a more general idea that, given our capacity for foresight and imagination, we are continuously being influenced by the ground plan of the life cycle as we begin to experience and conceive of it from childhood onward, and as it peaks to consciousness in adolescence and young adulthood. One of the functions of psychoanalytic insight is to reveal our experience and conception of this ground plan—for example, when we are expected to be the subservient, or assertive, woman or man, how we unconsciously begin rebelling against this vaguely perceived destiny, and experience loss and pain in our individuating not only from our specific parents and family but from the security of the ground plan of our subculture. (Note the dismal fate of Doya's husband in this regard.)

To the Editors:

I would like to comment on Dr. Kasin's excellent and thought provoking analysis of the dilemma of today's young person. (This Journal, volume 8, No. 1).

If Dr. Kasin's thesis is correct, viz., that "our youth suffer—from an ill-defined sense of fear of abandonment by the society they so urgently require to achieve their new mutuality needs, " then it becomes important to understand the reason behind society's perceived inability to come through for them. The beginning of the answer to that question is implied in Dr. Kasin's distinction between the authoritarian and "permissive" parent and the consequent attenuation or augmentation of the possibilities to look at one's self and others and to create one's own unique attitude toward the world. I would like to suggest that the authoritarian parent limits his own and other's freedom because the awareness of that freedom is terrifying.

When the child initially experiences his capacity to perform an autonomous act, it is exhilarating but also panicking because in some sense he has awareness of separation and I believe, in some way, perhaps archetypal, a foretaste of the ultimate separation, death. This may be the most frightening aspect of death. The fright itself, the felt expression of the idea of death, may be primarily separation anxiety—an awareness that no matter how extensive the security operations a person develops, there will ultimately come a time of separation.

The experiencing of one's own freedom is a reminder that nothing in living is inevitable—not even the neurotic symptoms which serve to perpetuate the myth that "things will always be this way." Resistance, incidentally, can be looked at from this point of view.

Gerard Chrzanowski M.D.

Gerard Chrzanowski

Gerard Chrzanowski, M.D.
250 East 87th St.
New York, N.Y. 10028

Gerard Chrzanowski  

TRANSCULTURAL PSYCHIATRY is a discipline that is approximately as old as the field of psychoanalysis. Kraepelin is usually credited with first studying the correlation of culture and mental illness. Freud, Jung, and Adler, independently of Kraepelin, and each from his own vantage point, developed an interest in the connections between cultural phenomena and neurotic or psychotic manifestations. Then came the era of the so-called cultural schools of psychoanalysis, which include Horney, Sullivan, Kardiner, and others. Attempting to transcend the intrapsychic aspects of mental disorders, they placed increasing emphasis on particular modes of acculturation and socialization in the genesis of psychopathology. Around the same time an interdisciplinary approach emerged; anthropologists, psychiatrists, psychoanalysts, behaviorists, and other experts in the social sciences worked together as teams. The height of that particular form of collaboration occurred in the 1930's and 1940's. Unfortunately, a period of latency followed. In recent years there has been renewed interest in cross-cultural and transcultural psychiatry. Thus far no consensus on acceptable standards, procedures, and goals for the discipline has been achieved.

It has become customary to speak of transcultural psychiatry (according to Ruesch and Wittkower) as a branch of social psychiatry. As such, it focuses mainly on those cultural factors that are related to the aetiology, frequency, and nature of mental disorders, and the care and aftercare of emotionally maladjusted people within the confines of a given cultural unit. The term cross-cultural ordinarily applies to comparisons of one culture with another. Transcultural is a more global term, implying an observational platform that transcends specific cultures. In addition, there is emerging an international psychiatry. This is concerned more specifically with teaching and training facilities in the psychiatric specialty, and also encompasses administrative problems, the supply and demand of qualified specialists and paraprofessionals, and treatment techniques without specific reference to the cultures involved.

IT WAS with a sense of humility and pride that I accepted the invitation to participate in the Harry Stack Sullivan Memorial Lecture series. I speak with modesty because I bring no original discoveries. I am proud to be here because Sullivan and the people around him had a more profound influence on my professional and personal life than any subsequent training experience. Perhaps that training period approached what Sullivan referred to as a "restitutive experience"—albeit in a prolonged adolescence. While I was originally attracted to Chestnut Lodge by Frieda Fromm-Reichmann and some of her excellent lectures, it was Harry Stack Sullivan who provided a bridge between my mid-Western pragmatism and the more theoretical aspects of psychoanalysis.

His concept of the interpersonal field as a source of solid evidence provided a generation of psychiatrists and behavioral scientists with the promise of testing psychological and sociological theories against behavioral and clinical observations. In short, he provided a methodological basis for the subsequent growth of ego psychology, social psychology, and cultural anthropology. His methodological concepts had intellectual impact upon behavioral science, which is perhaps as important in retrospect as his making the understanding of schizophrenia a respectable pursuit for psychiatrists.

PSYCHOANALYSIS IS NOT DEAD as long as observable phenomena remain the object of critical reformulation and clearer conceptualization. Dr. Schimel's article bears testimony to this in its intent and its execution. It also lends itself to criticism and clarification.

I shall confine my remarks to an appraisal of what may be reductionistic in the proposition that obsessionalism is essentially, if not exclusively, a stress-conditioned episode in the career line of the negativistic and/or the incorrigible personality in Sullivan's scheme of developmental disorders. I shall raise some questions, as well, in regard to related matters of other personality developments and pertinent disorders.

To begin with, I believe that the "obsessional's continued dedication to Power-Over and his hopes for dominance in interpersonal affairs" are not necessarily overlooked by the "sentimental" view of the infant or the child as a victim of manipulative parents, unless the patient or the therapist make a fetish out of this, or an ultimate explanation and justification. The question is rather why what was a necessity in the past continues to be a habit in the present, and purports to be a virtue for the future. This view is compatible with seeing the obsessional as attributing extraordinary power to words and ideas, having to know before he has an opportunity to learn, needing to be right no matter what, thus doubting any decision he is called upon to make.

Jay Lefer  

FROM THE FIRST PATIENTS treated by the psychoanalytic method, the "mysterious leap of the mind to the body" (Freud, 1955) has puzzled many. The analytic exploration of somatizing patients, as Engel (1968) noted, can be the "best source of material for gaining insight into the unconscious determinants and the metapsychology of the critical psychic states involved with the genesis of somatic disorder."

Two patients suffering from rheumatoid arthritis, depression, and obsessive-paranoid disorders were treated in psychoanalysis. Throughout the course of each analysis, my aim was to participate in an unfolding without the comfortable feeling that all was or could be understood in terms of Cartesian or psychological hydrodynamic frames of reference (Stainbrook, 1964).

These cases are presented to learn more about the physiology, familial, interpersonal, and intra-psychic aspects of the disease. Scheflen's (1969) admonition is valuable. Disappointment may follow those "who try to make simple one-to-one correlations between psychic and somatic variables. The problem is that they have been studying them whatever their theory from different levels of organization. To study a system we may break it down into parts as a step in the investigation, then synthesize to examine organization. There are no independent variables in a system."

The etiology of rheumatoid arthritis is unknown (Robinson, 1966). Research has failed to substantiate infectious, endocrine, autonomic nervous system, or genetic origins.

ONE KIND OF EMERGENCY in a general hospital setting, by far the most common, is the request for psychiatric consultation. This has as its aim the restoration of ward equilibrium by enabling the ward staff to perform their healing functions or by transferring the problem patient to a more appropriate facility. Unlike the traditional psychiatric consultation, which aims at diagnosis and recommendations for treatment based on evaluation of the individual patient, this type of consultation takes into account problems that arise among members of the hospital staff as well as the family and community members interacting with the patient. Disruption of this small but complex group, with the patient as its identified central element, becomes the object for reparative intervention by an outside agency, set up in a facility, called the Hospital Liaison Psychiatry Service (HLPS). HLPS intervention is the first step toward the restoration of mature collaboration, and the acceptance of realistic limitations within a hierarchical dependency culture.1

INTRODUCTION TO SOMEONE BECOMING A PATIENT

SEVERAL YEARS AGO I was asked to see in consultation a seventeen-year-old girl who was a patient in the medical section of a general hospital.

For two or three months prior to hospitalization, the girl (Kay) had been noted by her parents to be increasingly preoccupied, withdrawn, and seemingly depressed. Although she insisted that there was "nothing wrong" with her, after much urging she did consent to meet with a school counselor. During the fourth interview with this man Kay became mute, sitting with her eyes closed, her muscles rigid, and saliva drooling from the corner of her mouth. She did not visibly respond to a physician or her parents, and after about four hours in this withdrawn state she was transferred to a hospital, where she was examined by a neurologist who found no evidence of organic disturbance other than a minor elevation of cerebrospinal fluid protein and a slight—and transient—weakness of the left arm and leg. Kay spoke on the third day of hospitalization, but it was reported that what she said "didn't make much sense." I visited Kay during the second week of her hospital stay.

Alone in the room, propped up in bed, was a small, blonde girl, a large toy stuffed animal held close to her by her right arm, three fingers of her left hand in her mouth, and her eyes tightly closed. She at first made no response to my presence.

SUMMARY

In this paper I have tried, by means which include the verbatim quotation of a recorded extract from a psychoanalytic session, to show that a "here and now" approach, without reference to the patient's past, overcomes objections which are commonly brought against the possibility of using the psychoanalytic session as an experimental situation in which hypotheses about human behavior can be tested.

To the Editors:

Interpersonal relations without individuality again.

In the exchange on Harry Stack Sullivan in the last number of This Journal [Vol. 8, No. 1, Fall 1971, pp. 64–81], one participant, Dr. Ralph Crowley, saw fit to introduce some unrelated personal remarks as part of his reply (pp. 80–81). They, of course, do not affect the substantive issues. Instead of responding to them, I would, therefore, like to remind the interested reader of passages in Sullivan's Conceptions of Modern Psychiatry that indicate the absence of individuality from interpersonal relations.

First, from the Foreword to the third White Psychiatric Foundation printing (1947), page vi, third paragraph:

Gordon Allport and H. S. Odbert some years ago listed 17, 953 words used to indicate alleged qualities of human individuality … I have inveighed against "the delusion of unique individuality" and referred to personality as the hypothetical entity which we posit to account for interpersonal relations. I do not believe that this denies anyone "a personality"; it serves its purpose if it warns anyone that I never expect to know all about his personality—and am as certain as can be that he too will always share my ignorance in that regard.

to the last paragraph of the page that ends on the next:

Without digressing on the value of the comparative approach in formulating noncultural and especially nonlanguage aspects of living, I seek here to stress the central fact that the true or absolute individuality of a person is always beyond scientific grasp and invariably much less significant in the person's living than he has been taught to believe.

And second, from the paragraph on page 5, first printed in 1940 and, without change, reprinted in 1945 and 1947, that begins:

The unique individuality of the other fellow need never concern us as scientists.

Readers are invited to send in brief commentaries or critical evaluations of issues raised in this Journal or in the psychoanalytic field in general. These communications should be no more than five pages, and should be addressed to the Editors.

Margaret Rioch

Margaret J. Rioch, Ph.D.
4607 Dorset Avenue

Margaret Rioch  

DR. EZRIEL'S PAPER is a clear statement of the use of the "here and now" situation in psychoanalysis. It is refreshing to have pointed our so lucidly and cogently that the observations in the therapeutic situation are the only real data with which the analyst can work since everything else is necessarily an edited account of past events or speculation. It takes a great deal of rigorous self-discipline for a therapist to hold to the use of the very effective tool of transference as defined in this paper. It is the same discipline that is required in the self-study groups initiated by Wilfred Bion and continued in the Group Relations Conferences sponsored by the Centre for Applied Social Research of the Tavistock Institute of London, the Washington School of Psychiatry in the United States, and certain other institutions.

Like all purists Dr. Ezriel, in my opinion, limits the field unnecessarily and loses sight of the therapeutic value that other approaches have for patients even though they are not based so firmly on hard data. Dr. Ezriel's "laws" are very useful ways of conceptualizing much that occurs in psychoanalysis. At the same time they do not take account of the fact that not all of a patient's behavior is neurotic and does not, therefore, fall into the categories of the three kinds of object relationships he mentions. It does make sense to think of a patient's neurotic behavior as an avoidance of a kind of relationship which he fears because he thinks it will lead to calamity. But in avoiding one kind of relationship, the patient still has an option of many other kinds of relationship. The "required" relationship is thus not completely understandable in terms of avoidance alone. Other factors play a role in bringing about the particular kind of behavior which the patient "chooses" (obviously not as a conscious choice) to replace the repressed.

In spite of these reservations, I find Dr. Ezriel's work a model of an intelligent, scientific approach to therapeutic work.

Psychoanalytic Reflections on Women's Liberation

Ruth Moulton M.D.

Ruth Moulton

Ruth Moulton, M.D.
285 Central Park West
New York, N.Y. 10024

Ruth Moulton  

UNTIL LAST YEAR, I paid little attention to the Women's Liberation Movement. It seemed to represent either a rerun of what I had lived with for forty-five years or an embarrassing overstatement of that experience. Then in August 1970 on a remote Greek island, as I was reading a news report on the fiftieth anniversary of the Women's Suffrage Act, the photograph of a placard carried in a Women's Liberation demonstration caught my eye. The placard read: "Down with women who have made it." It struck me that the demonstrators probably included me in that characterization. These women of the new generation, I realized, would hate me as a smug renegade who refused to fight openly, satisfied with her own modicum of success and indifferent to their dilemma because it was no longer mine. My justification for my current lack of involvement might have been that I had already done my share. Had I not proved, alone and in my own way, that a woman could combine marriage and motherhood with a professional career? But then I proceeded to ask myself if that was really the full measure of my share. Perhaps it behooves those of us who have "made it" to cease to regard ourselves as "above" the present struggle and try to make a contribution. To start with, we might review for ourselves how we had handled the same dilemma.

Presented to the William Alanson White Psychoanalytic Society on September 22, 1971.

Leah Davidson  

IF SULLIVAN'S tenet "We are all more simply human than otherwise" is valid, then the problem of understanding attitudes and behavior, particularly those we come to consider anomalous, in different social structures, becomes a matter of the inquirer's orientation. Too often, we have assumed erroneously that behavior patterns that are similar, or analogous, have the same meaning. On the shock of discovery of our error, we retreat into our caves of pessimism, doubting we can communicate cross-culturally. It is obvious that behaviors that are analogous may or may not be related to each other. Our understanding, on the other hand, is enhanced when we examine homologous (not analogous) forms. That is, to fully comprehend, without substituting metaphor for insight, we have to appreciate private experience and examine its fit in the structural patterning of relationships between persons. The process of behavior is a sign of a relationship between one object and another. This interactive process, and the relationship of these processes, is what Sullivan emphasized in his attempts at defining the interpersonal.

This group of essays, inspired by the Indian film "Devi, " directed by Satyajit Ray, is based on presentations at a meeting of the Harry Stack Sullivan Society on March 21, 1970, and on a round table discussion that was conducted on December 4, 1970 at the annual winter meeting of the American Academy of Psychoanalysis. G. Chrzanowski, M.D., was chairman of the round table discussion, held under the auspices of the Workshop on Transcultural Psychiatry.

Ruth Moulton  

DESPITE THE UNIQUE aspect of Indian culture and the vast differences between Indian concepts of the role of women and the family and our own, I am struck by how well this film demonstrates some of the more universal conflicts of women. It shows dramatically how a girl can be trapped between the universal need for a "good earth" mother, a magic source of life and healing, and the tendency we have to turn on her and view her as destructive, evil, and withholding when she fails to live up to these irrational expectations. The dilemma of a young woman who has been infantilized and overprotected as a beautiful child and is then suddenly expected to be mother of us all, is especially poignant in the case of Doya, who came as a child-bride to an upper-class household, where there was no mother-in-law to train her to be an adequate wife and mother. With her own husband away at school, she becomes overly dependent on her father-in-law, thus illustrating her enormous need for a parent. The old man's loneliness and need for a wife makes the symbiosis more binding. Doya is depressed at being childless, but gets gratification from mothering her father-in-law and young nephew.

As the most submissive and helpless member of the household, her deification serves her need for self-validation, as well as gratifying the father-in-law's need for a magic mother. While this magic solution has cultural and religious backing in India, it also parallels the complaints of the many American women who feel they also need to be devoted and subservient. Some feel they are put on a pedestal, glorified, and idealized only to be exploited and enchained. They feel that men seduce and worship them, yet add the unrealistic burdens of being a wife and mother at the same time. They are blamed if they do not produce perfect children a lá Spockian era.

Deification of a woman only leads to her crucifixion. Paddy Chayevsky in his movie "The Goddess" shows how deification of the American movie queen may lead to her downfall by giving rise to unrealizable and inconsistent expectations.

The Cultural Background

Bertram Schaffner M.D.

Bertram Schaffner

Bertram Schaffner, M.D.
220 Central Park South
New York, N.Y. 10019

Bertram Schaffner  

IT IS EXTREMELY difficult for a Westerner to understand the events of "Devi" without an introduction to the historical and cultural setting in which the events take place. The internal and external struggles which so profoundly affect the equilibrium and destiny of the characters intertwined in the story are determined by factors originating in the Hindu religion, in the India of that particular time in history, and in the winds of social change at that time.

The story takes place in Bengal about a century ago, when Romo Han Roy founded a movement of religious reform, based upon scientific enlightenment, that particularly opposed traditions by which a father wielded total, irrational authority over the family. The setting is a wealthy household, whose members live in striking contrast to thousands of hungry ill-clad poor who come to worship the new goddess. The story symbolizes the power of religion over rich and poor alike, owing to lack of education, submissiveness to tradition and superstition, and fear of divine reprisal for opposition to religious rules and traditions.

The film reveals the primitive state of medical care at the time in rural India, the local doctors' own sense of the inadequacy of the means at their disposal, and their fear of opposing the popular belief in the healing powers of the goddess Kali.

The lines of worshippers who come to see the new goddess include chronically ill of all types, blind, lame, amputated, infected, debilitated; obviously, they are inadequately cared for by local medical facilities. Like many rural populations under such conditions, they lived in dread of disease, and clung tenaciously to a religion that promised them some hope of cure or relief. The film not so subtly shows the inability of religion to deal with physical illness, which in this case appears to be the dreaded cholera.

At the time of the "Devi" story, English was regarded in Han Roy's reform circles as the essential tool for acquiring the new rational scientific approach to deal with India's problems.

THESE COMMENTS are stimulated by Dr. Moulton's reference to the failure of women to fulfill their promise after gaining admission to many spheres from which they were previously barred. She quotes Cynthia Epstein's statement on the tendency of highly trained women to "underperform, underachieve and underproduce." For example, many more women choose a career in nursing rather than medicine, or choose to be nursery-school teachers rather than college teachers. How do we account for this fact? As analysts we know that external discrimination does not adequately explain it.

As a result of cultural pressures from birth, most women accept the neurotically dependent, self-effacing solution in life. (I use the terms dependent and self-effacing as described by Karen Horney.) In fact, this is the character pattern that most cultures consider normal and refer to as "feminine." It is not a superficial social facade, but rather a profound, deeply rooted neurotic personality pattern in which the individual subordinates himself to others, becomes dependent on them, and spends most of his energies searching for help, protection, and love. When this happens, certain impulses and behavior are taboo, and others are highly valued. The qualities of love and lovableness become of highest importance, and from childhood on, he or she works hard at developing the type of personality which, it is felt, will be most acceptable to others. The individual tries to be agreeable, sympathetic, and compassionate, avoiding friction or disagreement. Since he anxiously needs love and acceptance from others, he will go to any lengths to get it. Above all, such an individual must not antagonize anyone. Therefore, he rigidly represses any impulse which may be construed by others as hostile.

Inevitably, certain unfortunate complications develop. By suppressing all impulses that could be regarded by others as hostile, he also suppresses spontaneity and has great difficulty with self-assertion. This will show itself in small ways as well as large.

Silvano Arieti  

ABOUT TEN YEARS AGO I had the honor and the pleasure of discussing at the William Alanson White Institute a paper by Dr. Otto Will. It was a wonderful paper, but as wonderful as that paper was, as well as the others that Dr. Will has written since then, this paper is even more profound, and of a scope so large as not to be easily grasped at a first reading of it.

Perhaps I am biased. After all, catatonia has been a particular interest of mine since my first contacts with psychiatry. Moreover, I have witnessed with disappointment in the several decades of my involvement with psychiatry an almost total neglect of the field of catatonia on the part of the psychiatric and psychoanalytic profession. And yet in my opinion nothing could be more revealing of the nadir of the human condition than the study of catatonia. In addition to all the usual psychodynamic conflicts, the drama of man appears here fully in his ethical dimension: to do or not to do. As I wrote elsewhere (Arieti, 1967) the catatonic "lives only in the fear of what he could do, and the only choice left to him which he thinks he is not choosing, is not to do."

With great mastery Dr. Will portrays the drama in the case of Kay.
